  "text": "In the morning Tobias took the church road again. He carried Maren’s bread, which the baker had given him without asking whether he was going that way.

There was wind now. It moved the grass beside the posts. At the eleventh he stopped and shifted the loaf under his arm, keeping its folded paper clear of a nail.

The door was shut.

He knocked with two knuckles. In the pause afterward he heard the paper crackle where his hand had tightened. He loosened it.

Through the front window he could see the lamp on the sill. Unlit. The rug lay straight before the hearth. Maren had always left one corner turned where the door caught it; he had watched her push it back with her heel, carrying tea.

He went no nearer the glass.

There was a place beside the step where deliveries stayed dry. He bent to leave the loaf there, then stood with it still in his hand.

At church he sat in the last pew. When the others rose, he rose. When they sat, he remained standing a moment longer, until someone touched his sleeve.

Afterward he took the bread home and put it on his table.

By evening the paper had dried stiff around it. He unfolded the corners carefully. A little sand fell out onto the boards.

Tobias fetched the brush. Then he fetched the pan.

He had almost swept it up when he stopped to count the small wet marks beneath his chair.",

  "text": "There were eleven. By the time Tobias counted again, two had dried.

He set the pan beside the stove and leaned the brush against it. The bread remained on the table, opened but uncut. He covered it with a cloth before going upstairs.

In the night he heard the chair move.

It was a sound he knew: one short scrape, then another, because the rear leg caught between the boards. He had meant to mend that leg before winter. Lying still, he remembered where he kept the glue.

Nothing else happened.

At first light he came down carrying his shoes. The chair stood tucked beneath the table. He could not remember whether he had left it so.

He put on his shoes by the door.

Outside, the road was firm with cold. He walked past the baker’s without looking in and took the turning toward the church. At the eleventh post a strip of paper fluttered on the nail. He freed it carefully. There was no writing on either side.

Maren’s door was shut. He stood before it until his hands grew cold, then folded the paper and put it in his pocket.

On his way home he bought glue.

He worked on the chair all afternoon. When he had finished, he tested it with his weight, rising and sitting, listening. It no longer made a sound.

For supper he cut two slices from the loaf. He put one back beneath the cloth.

Then he moved the chair a little farther from the table, so there was room to sit without drawing it out.",

  "text": "The glue dried white where it had squeezed from the joint. In the morning Tobias pared it away with his pocketknife. He gathered the curls in his palm and carried them to the stove.

The second slice lay beneath the cloth. He ate it standing up.

For three nights he heard nothing. On the fourth there was a small sound from below, not the chair but something set upon the table. He waited until daylight before going down.

His cup stood beside the loaf. He usually left it on the shelf, though not always.

He washed it and put it away.

That afternoon he went to Maren’s with a piece of bread wrapped in paper. He knocked once. From inside came the ordinary stillness of a house whose windows were shut.

He left the bread on the step, then returned for it before reaching the gate. There were dogs along that road.

At home he found the blank paper in his coat. One fold had begun to tear. He smoothed it beneath his cup and ate the bread he had brought back.

The days shortened. He stopped counting the marks by the stove. Sometimes he wiped them up; sometimes the fire did it for him.

Once, passing the table with an armful of wood, he struck the empty chair with his knee.

He apologized before he could help it.

Then he stood holding the wood. A piece of bark fell against his shoe.

He bent to pick it up, and when he straightened he left the chair where it was.",
